## Today's dataset

![2021 *AJPS*](officers.png)

## We'll start by reading in the data

```{webr}
officerdata <- read.csv('officers.csv')
head(officerdata) # head() shows the first six rows of a longer dataset.
```

:::{.notes}
search_occur: whether or not a search was conducted by the officer at that stop

contra: whether or not contraband was found by the officer at that stop

driver_age: age of driver (years)

driver_race: race of driver (white, poc)

officer_female: officer gender
:::

# What if we just want data on stops by female officers?

## We need to *subset* our data

Like this:

`name.of.new.subset.dataset <- subset(original.dataset, variable.in.dataset == accepted.value)`

- If the variable is a **string,** wrap `accepted.value` in quotations, like this: `== 'accepted.value'`
- Note `==`
  - this is a **boolean operator**

## An aside on boolean operators

<table>
<tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Tests that return a <code>TRUE</code> or <code>FALSE</code> value</strong></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>==</code></td><td>is equal to</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>&lt;</code> and <code>&gt;</code></td><td>is less than/greater than</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>&lt;=</code> and <code>&gt;=</code></td><td>is less than/greater than <em>or equal to</em></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>!=</code></td><td>is not equal to</td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Combining boolean operations</strong></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>&amp;</code></td><td>and</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>|</code> (bar)</td><td>or</td></tr>
</table>

## Remember our `belchers` dataset:

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
belchers <- read.csv('belchers.csv')
belchers
```

Let's subset to Belchers 18 and up:

```{webr}
# subset(original.dataset, variable.in.dataset == accepted.value)
adult.belchers <- 
adult.belchers
```

:::{.notes}
adult.belchers is an entirely new dataset, and we can do all the things with it that we could do to belchers.
:::

## How would we subset to only Belchers who are students?

```{r, echo = F}
belchers <- read.csv('belchers.csv')
belchers
```

```{webr}
student.belchers <- 
student.belchers
```

:::{.notes}
Note use of quotes around "Student"!
:::

## A more serious example

Let's subset `officerdata` to only stops by female officers.

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
officerdata <- read.csv('officers.csv')
```

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
head(officerdata, 3) # you can specify the number of rows in head()!
```

(Remember: `officer_female` is a **binary indicator.**)


```{webr}
female.officers <- 
head(female.officers)
```

:::{.notes}
subset(officerdata, officer_female==1)
:::

## Now let's subset to only data on *searches* conducted by *female officers.*

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
officerdata <- read.csv('officers.csv')
```

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
head(officerdata, 3)
```

You can subset on more than one variable! Use a **boolean operator.**

```{webr}
female.officer.stops <- 
head(female.officer.stops)
```

## Using `mean()` within a subset

Let's compare the rate of contraband found among stops by female and non-female (male?) officers.

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
officerdata <- read.csv('officers.csv')
```

```{webr}
female.officer.stops <- subset(officerdata, officer_female == 1 & search_occur == 1)
mean(female.officer.stops$contra)
```

```{webr}
nonfemale.officer.stops <- 
mean(nonfemale.officer.stops$contra)
```

## What we have covered

- `head()` shows you the first six rows of a dataset
- `subset()` lets you extract a portion of the data based on the value of one or more variables
- **Boolean operators** like `==`, `>=`, and `&` are how you specify the values you want
- Review: `mean()` gives you the average value of a numeric variable
